meta.title: Who really said "Tell me and I forget. Teach me and I may remember. Involve me and I learn"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No, Benjamin Franklin didn’t say it. The line is a 20th-century evolution of a Chinese proverb rooted in Xunzi; the Franklin credit only surfaces in the 1980s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Tell me and I forget. Teach me and I may remember. Involve me and I learn'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Franklin. The three-part saying evolved from an old Chinese proverb tracing back to Xunzi; the Franklin attribution is a 1980s error.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Franklin — a modern proverb wrongly pinned on him
answer.authorDates: c. 310 – c. 235 BCE · Chinese Confucian philosopher (ancestral source of the idea, not the wording)
answer.sourceLine: There is no substantive evidence Benjamin Franklin ever wrote or spoke this line; his name only became attached to it in the 1980s. As Quote Investigator traces, the saying is a 20th-century evolution of an older “Chinese proverb” family whose oldest documented ancestor is a passage in the Xunzi (3rd c. BCE), which entered English through Homer H. Dubs’ 1928 translation. The exact three-part “Tell me … involve me and I learn” wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase, not a verbatim line from Xunzi or Franklin.

source.excerpt: Tell me and I forget. Teach me and I may remember. Involve me and I learn.
trail: The oldest known ancestor is a passage in the Xunzi stressing that hearing is inferior to seeing, seeing less than knowing, and knowing less than putting into practice — rendered into English by Homer H. Dubs in 1928, per Quote Investigator.

Through the 1950s–70s the line circulated as a “Chinese proverb” (e.g. 1974: “Tell me, I forget; show me, I remember; involve me, I understand”), only later hardening into the familiar triad, as QI documents year by year.
Benjamin Franklin first received credit only in 1986, and Franklin scholars H. W. Brands and Thomas Kidd told Check Your Fact they had never encountered it in his writings.
source.excerptNote: The wording circulates in many forms — “teach me and I remember,” “show me and I remember,” “involve me and I understand” — a hallmark of a proverb that evolved by retelling rather than a fixed line by a single author.
source.rightsNote: The exact modern wording is an anonymous 20th-century paraphrase with no identifiable single author, so no copyright status can be asserted for it. Its ancient ancestor in the Xunzi is public-domain in the original Chinese, and Homer H. Dubs’ 1928 English translation is a distinct, differently-worded text.

author.name: Xunzi (Xun Kuang)
author.heading: Where the idea really comes from
author.metaLine: c. 310 – c. 235 BCE · Chinese Confucian philosopher
author.bio: Xunzi (Xun Kuang) was a leading Confucian thinker of the late Warring States period, known for a rigorous, this-worldly ethics and for teaching that character is cultivated through practice and ritual rather than innate goodness. The Xunzi chapter Ruxiao contains the oft-cited progression — hearing is less than seeing, seeing less than knowing, knowing less than doing — that later English writers loosely reshaped into the modern “Tell me … involve me and I learn” proverb. He did not, however, write the wording popularly quoted today.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented ancestor: Xunzi, “Ruxiao,” trans. Homer H. Dubs, The Works of Hsüntze (London: Arthur Probsthain, 1928). misattribution.heading: How Franklin got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet name” misattribution: a warm, quotable line about hands-on learning drifted onto Benjamin Franklin decades after it was already circulating anonymously.

items.why: Franklin’s name only appears on this saying from 1986 onward, with no source in his own writings. Scholars H. W. Brands and Thomas Kidd told Check Your Fact they had never seen it and found it “very un-Franklin.”
From the 1950s the line spread as a generic “Chinese proverb” and was sometimes tied to Confucius, but Quote Investigator traces the documented root to the Xunzi, not the Analects.
A 1993 instance recast it as a Native American saying — one more floating label attached to a proverb with no fixed author, per QI.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: an anonymous 20th-century proverb, evolved from a Chinese-philosophy tradition rooted in the Xunzi — and not Benjamin Franklin’s words.

context.heading: Why the phrasing keeps shifting
lead: The line has no stable text because it was never authored once and quoted since — it was re-said across decades. Compilers swapped “show” for “teach,” “understand” for “learn,” and “I forget” for “I will forget,” each retelling smoothing it toward a tidy triad.

That drift is the tell of a proverb, not a quotation. When a saying attaches to Franklin, Confucius, and “a Native American elder” in different sources, the safe inference is that it belongs to none of them individually and to the tradition collectively.
context.detailsSummary: The Xunzi passage it descends from
detailsBody: Homer H. Dubs’ 1928 translation of the Xunzi renders the idea as a ladder: not having heard is less than having heard, hearing less than seeing, seeing less than knowing, and knowing less than putting it into practice. The modern proverb compresses that ladder into three memorable beats — but the compression, and the crediting to Franklin, are 20th-century additions.
context.pull: A quote has one wording; a proverb has many. This one has many.
